newsitem.title: UK: London shares set for week of range trading.
newsitem.headline: London shares set for week of range trading.

text.p: The UK share market next week could be in-line for a repeat performance of the past week and is unlikely to stage any major upturn as institutional players remain in the wings due to worries about Wall Street and the looming British election.

Concerns that the Dow may be on the verge of another downturn as well as fear that a Labour government will hike corporate taxes in order to plug a gaping hole in UK finances has kept many fund managers away the past week, resulting in low volumes and tight trading ranges.
"Our (institutional) clients have gone to sleep and I don't expect them to stir until next month," the head of trading at a major brokerage said.
"The main task next week will be trying to stay awake."

The FTSE 100, which has been confined to a daily trading range of 20 to 30 points over the past five sessions and struggled to push turnover above 600 million shares, should see some increased activity on Monday due to a sizeable flotation.

The Alliance & Leicester Building Society is expected to hit the market with a price tag of between 480 pence and 520 pence a share, according to broker BZW, valuing the company at around 2.5 billion stg.
While institutional appetite for the Alliance & Leicester may inflate overall FTSE volume, the index itself is not expected to derive much benefit.
"I really can't see the FTSE making much headway. The fundamental and technical picture is still quite bearish," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International.
Political as well as economic uncertainties will continue to act as a drag on investor sentiment, preventing the FTSE from making much headway beyond the 4,330-4,335 level, Shah said.

Labour, which is currently leading the ruling Conservatives by around 20 percentage points in opinion polls, is pledged to place a windfall tax on utilities but some strategists think they may not stop there.
Richard Kersley, strategist at broker BZW fears Labour, if elected, would be confronted with a 10 billion stg hole in Britain's "fragile" finances.
Kersley believes a Labour government will "make adjustments" in corporate taxes in order to raise up to five billion stg -- something that hasn't been taken into current share price valuations.
The strong pound, which is trading at near five year highs against major European currencies, will also cause investors a few headaches in the coming months, Shah said.
"Sterling's strength has already hit corporate profitability and that is set to continue right through next year," Shah said.
On Wednesday, Reed International Plc and Reuters Holdings Plc became the latest in a growing list of UK corporates who have warned the strong pound is likely to inhibit earnings growth.
Sterling's strength may feature in SmithKline Beecham's first-quarter figures, due for release on Tuesday.

In the full-year to 31 December 1996, the pharmaceuticals group derived 3.885 billion stg, or 49 percent of its revenues, from the U.S. while 1.83 billion stg, or 23 percent, came from sales in continental Europe, according to data from Reuters Securities 3000.
Domestic considerations aside, UK investors may also have to come to grips with another possible downturn on Wall Street in the coming weeks, strategists said.
Chris Chaitow, technical analyst, said the Dow's recent strength was merely a technical bounce from an oversold position and would falter by mid-May.
"The bears will again gain the upper hand," Chaitow said, adding that there was little to stop the Dow from plunging to around the 5,500 level by the end of the summer.
In addition to SmithKline, ICI Plc is due to report first-quarter figures next week. Amongst second-liners, Bank of Scotland Plc and Eurotunnel Plc publish full-year figures.
Economic statistics due for release include UK retail sales and trade deficit figures.
